Cheat sheets and review notes for CBE 142, chemical kinetics and reactor design (UC Berkeley). 24 handwritten pages: the midterm 1 cheat sheet (pages 1–6), a review (“The legend”) (pages 7–8), the final review (pages 9–13), the midterm 2 review (pages 14–16), a second set of design-equation notes (pages 17–23) and the final crib sheet (page 24). See also the two-page crib sheet.

Page 3 — energy balance: equilibrium conversion

For a reversible reaction, Xe​ is the maximum conversion that can be achieved at the reaction temp.

E.g. N2​O4​⇌2NO2​: Kc​=[N2​O4​][NO2​]2​=CA​CB2​​. From the stoich. table, CA​=CA0​(1−XA​), CB​=2CA0​XA​ ∴ Kc​=CA0​(1−XA​)4CA02​XA2​​=(1−XA​)4CA0​XA2​​ ∴ (this is the equilibrium conversion)

Xe​=XA​=4CA0​Kc​(1−XA​)​​​

For a first-order reversible reaction A⇌B: Kc​=CA​CB​​=CA0​(1−XA​)CA0​(XA​)​; Kc​(1−XA​)=XA​; Kc​−Kc​XA​=XA​ ⇒ Xe​=XA​=1+Kc​Kc​​​

The equilibrium conversion is dependent on T of the reactor ↳ for an exothermic reaction, as T↑, Kc​↓ and therefore Xe​↓.

When solving questions that are non-isothermal, it is important to understand that Kc​, Xe​ and XEB​ are all temp. dependent:

  • Xe​ → mole balance; XEB​ → energy balance } the intersection of these two provides the adiabatic equilibrium Te​ and Xe​ (reactor conditions).

(sketch: X vs. T — the falling equilibrium curve Xe​=1+Kc​(T)Kc​(T)​ from 1.0 and the rising energy-balance line crossing at (Te​,Xe​).)

XEB​=−ΔHR​∑Θcp​(T−T0​)​(for adiabatic reactor)=−ΔHRx​cpA​​(T−T0​)​(constant cp​)}linear equation

Page 4 — energy balance equations

Energy Acc.=Q˙​−W˙+energy in−energy out;dtdE^sys​​=Q˙​−W˙+i=1∑n​Ei​Fi​​in​−i=1∑n​Ei​Fi​​out​;Ei​=Ui​+2ui2​​+gzi​

W˙ = flow work (Fi​PVˉi​) + shaft work (W˙s​). If we let E=U & take Fi​ common, Fi​H(Ui​+PVˉ)​​, we get the energy balance as:

dtdE^sys​​=Q˙​−W˙s​+i=1∑n​Fi​Hi​​in​−i=1∑n​Fi​Hi​​out​

Expressing FA​=FA0​(1−XA​); FB​=FA0​(ΘB​−ab​X) & adding up enthalpies to give ΔHR​:

i=1∑n​Fi0​Hi0​−i=1∑n​Fi​Hi​=FA0​i=1∑n​Θi​(Hi0​−Hi​)−ΔHRx​(T)FA0​X ∴Q˙​−W˙s​+FA0​∑Θi​(Hi0​−Hi​)−ΔHRx​(T)FA0​X=0​→S.S.; for known H’s & ΔHR​; can be used for phase change

If no phase change: Hi​(T)=Hi∘​(Tref​)+∫Tref​T​cpi​​dT (reference temp. & enthalpies cancel); Hi​−Hi0​=∫Ti0​T​cpi​​dT≈cpi​​(T−Ti0​) → assuming cp​ ≠ T-dependent.

★∴Q˙​−W˙s​−FA0​∑Θcpi​​(T−Ti0​)−ΔHR​(T)FA0​X=0​★

→ S.S.; when cp​‘s are known but H is not known; no phase change; cp​ is constant w/ T. Where ΔHR​(T)=ΔHR∘​(Tref​)+Δcp​(T−Tref​).

Page 5 — adiabatic energy balance

W˙s​=0, Q˙​=0 & Ti0​=T0​: we can rearrange the previous OP OG equation to give:

X=−ΔHR​(T)∑Θi​cpi​​(T−T0​)​=−​ΔHR∘​(Tref​)+negligibleΔcp​(T−Tref​)​​​∑Θi​cpi​​(T−T0​)​≈−ΔHR∘​(Tref​)∑Θi​cpi​​(T−T0​)​​(linear plot)

(valid for BSTR, CSTR, PFR & PBR). (sketch: X rising linearly with T.) Solving for T:

T=∑Θi​cpi​​+XΔcp​X[−ΔHR∘​(Tref​)]+∑Θi​cpi​​T0​+XΔcp​TR​​​

This can now be used to solve for rA​. E.g. [PFR] Ak2​⇌k1​​​B:

−rA​=k1​CA​−k2​CB​=k1​[CA​−k1​k2​​CB​]=k1​[CA​−Kc​CB​​];k1​(T)=kexp[RE​(T0​1​−T1​)];Kc​(T)=Kexp[R−ΔHR∘​​(T0​1​−T1​)]

CA​=CA0​(1−X)TT0​​; CB​=CA0​XA​TT0​​ ∴ −rA​=kCA0​[(1−X)−Kc​X​]TT0​​.

∴ We have two knowns (X,V); eqns: (1) dVdX​=FA0​−rA​​; (2) k(T); (3) Kc​(T); (4) T(X) } ODE solver! If Δcp​=0=cpB​​−cpA​​: T=∑Θi​cpi​​X[−ΔHR∘​(Tref​)]​+T0​.

Page 6 — wall-cooled / heat exchangers w/ reactors

With the addition of extra heat, the energy balance will now include a Q term that is due to heating:

ΔQ˙​+∑Fi​Hi​​V​−∑Fi​Hi​​V+ΔV​=0;ΔQ˙​=UΔA(Ta​−T)=UaΔV(Ta​−T)

(U = heat trans. coeff.; ΔA = heat exchange area; Ta​ = ambient temp.; a=VA​=πD2L/4πDL​=D4​ = heat exchange area per unit volume.) Therefore the differential equation that we get:

Ua(Ta​−T)−dVd∑(Fi​Hi​)​=0⇒Ua(Ta​−T)−∑dVdFi​​Hi​−∑Fi​dVdHi​​=0;ΔH=cp​ΔT;dVdH​=cp​dVdT​ ∴dVdT​=∑Fi​cpi​​rA​ΔHR​−Ua(T−Ta​)​​=FA0​(∑Θi​cpi​​+Δcp​X)rA​ΔHR​−Ua(T−Ta​)​​PFR (steady state)

Qg​=rA​ΔHR​ (heat generated); QR​=Ua(T−Ta​) (heat removed).

Similarly, for a PBR (ρb​ → bulk density): dWdT​=∑Fi​cpi​​rA​ΔHR​−ρb​Ua(T−Ta​)​​.

EB on the heat-transfer fluid (c → coolant/heating medium) — not overall energy balances, just on the coolant:

  • Co-current: dVdTa​​=m˙c​cpc​​Ua(T−Ta​)​
  • Counter-current: dVdTa​​=m˙c​cpc​​Ua(Ta​−T)​

(sketch: bulk CA0​ → external diffusion → surface CAs​ → internal diffusion → CA​(r) inside a porous catalyst.)

−DAB​dr2d2CA​​+rA​=0[mole balance including diffusion and reaction]

(DAB​: ext. diffusion coefficient, in bulk fluid & BL.)

Effective diffusion: the catalyst itself has pores that twist/turn (tortuous). There are voids and solids of varying conc. and diffusion does not always occur normal to the direction of flux ↳ therefore we define an effective diffusion:

De​=τ~DAB​ϕp​σc​​​
  • DAB​ = bulk diffusivity; ϕp​ = porosity = total volumevolume of empty (voids)​
  • σc​ = constriction factor (accounts for variation in normal cross-section area)
  • τ~ = tortuosity = shortest distance possibleactual distance travelled​

rA​⇒[dm3smol​]; rA′​⇒[gcatalyst​smol​]; rA′′​⇒[m2smol​] ∴ −rA​=ρc​(−rA′​); −rA​=ρc​Sa​(−rA′′​) (ρc​ = g catalyst/volume; Sa​ = m²/g catalyst) ↳ this is the same for rate-constant units (k1​, k1′​, k1′′​).

Shell balance on porous catalyst: (sketch: a spherical shell between r and r+Δr.)

(In@r)−(Out@r+Δr)+(gen within Δr)=0;flux⋅area−flux⋅area+massrate​⋅ρc​⋅Vshell​⋅Δr=0 WA​×4πr2​r​−WA​×4πr2​r+Δr​+(rA′​⋅ρc​⋅4πrm2​Δr)=0(rm​=mean radius between r & r+Δr)

÷4πΔr & Δr→0 ⇒ drd(WA​r2)​−rA′​ρc​r2=0, with WA​=−De​drdCA​​ (moles of A/open-pore volume) and −rA′​=kn​kn′′​Sa​ρc​​​CAn​. Chain rule + dividing by r2De​:

∴dr2d2CA​​+r2​(drdCA​​)−De​kn​​CAn​=0​;BCs: at r=R,CA​=CAs​;r=0,drdCA​​=0

Now if we non-dimensionalize, ψ=CAs​CA​​; λ=Rr​; WA,r​=−De​drdCA​​=−d(Rλ)De​d(ψCAs​)​=−RDe​CAs​​dλdψ​. Doing this gives us:

dλ2d2ψ​+λ2​dλdψ​−this expression pops outDe​kn​R2CAsn−1​​​​ψn=0​⇒ϕn2​(Thiele modulus)=internal diffusion ratesurface rxn rate​;kn​=kn′′​Sa​ρc​

∴ ϕn​≫1: the reaction rate is very fast (internal diffusion limiting).

We can solve the above diff. eq. to get a solution for a first-order reaction:

ψ=λA1​​coshϕ1​λ+λB1​​sinhϕ1​λ⇒ψ=λ1​sinh(ϕ1​)sinh(ϕ1​λ)​

(sketch: ψ vs. r from R to 0 for increasing φ.) As φ↑, the rxn rate increases and therefore A reacts faster than it diffuses, going to zero @ the center.

Effectiveness factor. The reaction rate depends on conc.; the conc. depends on r along the catalyst. The rate also changes and the rate @ the surface is not the same as the rate in the middle } η (effectiveness factor):

η=max rate possible if everything is @ CAs​,Ts​actual rate​=MAs​MA​​(reaction rates, mol/s);MA​=−RDe​CAs​​dλdψ​​λ=1​(4πR2);MAs​=k1​CAs​(34​πR3)

We have to solve for η for every order by solving the diff. eq. (sketch: η vs. φ — falling from 1, zero order furthest right, then first order, then second order.) As φ decreases, η → 1 (surface rxn limited). ϕ∝R,De​1​,k; η∝ϕ1​.

We can express the rate in terms of φ: −rA​=(rate @ CAs​actual rate​)×(rate @ CAs​); −rA​=η(kCAs​); −rA​=η(−rAs​)​ — the effectiveness factor is a measure of surface accessibility.

As Φ=internal diffusion MTsurface rxn rate​, Φ≫1 means that the system is internal-diffusion limited (surface reaction happening super fast) ↓ in this limiting case, η can be approximated as:

η=(n+12​)1/2Φ3​​(Φ≫1);for a first order: η=Φ12​3​(Φ1​cothΦ1​−1)

Transcriber’s note: written as coth(Φ1​−1) in the original; the standard result is Φ1​cothΦ1​−1.

Chapter 14

  • For solid catalysts (non-porous) in a PBR we can just use the PBR balance: dWdFA​​=−rA​ (reaction happening only on the surface)
  • However, might need more info as −rA​=kCA,s​, but we don’t have an expression for CA,s​
  • This is where we use the fact that the reaction is external-diffusion limited ↳ the amount of A that diffuses to the surface reacts:
WA,r​=−rA′′​;kc​(CA,b​−CA,s​)=(k′′k′Sa​​​)CA,s​→CAs​=kr​+kc​kc​CA​​

→ can get an expression for CA,s​, which can be substituted in −rA​ to give dWdFA​​=−rA​:

∴−rAs′′​=kr​+kc​kc​kr​CA​​​;keff​=kr​+kc​kc​kr​​

We can do limiting cases to analyse what the rate is dependent on:

  1. When kr​≫kc​: −rAs′′​=kc​CA​. When Sc↑, we can just approximate Sh=0.6Re1/2Sc1/3 (for a sphere) ∴ kc​=0.6ν1/6DAB2/3​​⋅(dp​U​)1/2 → these will affect kc​ and therefore the reaction rate of A.

E.g. @ low U, diffusion limiting (big BL); @ high U, fast MT (could be reaction limiting) } for a fixed U, decreasing dp​ will result in high kc​ (fast MT).

Chapter 11 [adiabatic, non-isothermal reactors]

  1. ΔHRx​(T)=ΔHRx∘​(TR​)+Δcp​(T−TR​); Δcp​=c(cp​)products​−b(cp​)reactant​ (stoichiometric ratios)
  2. Q˙​−FA0​∑Θi​cpi​​(T−Ti0​)−[ΔHR∘​(TR​)+Δcp​(T−TR​)]FA0​X=0 [OP OG EB w/ W˙s​=0]
  3. XEB​=−[ΔHR∘​(TR​)+Δcp​(T−TR​)]∑Θi​cpi​​(T−T0​)​; Q˙​=0; W˙s​=0 (works for all reactors) (sketch: XEB​ linear in T.)
  4. ⇕ T=∑Θi​cpi​​+XΔcp​X[−ΔHRx∘​(TR​)]+∑Θi​cp​T0​+XΔcp​TR​​ Δcp​=0& feed is pure A​ T=T0​+cpA​​X[−ΔHRx∘​(TR​)]​
  5. Kc​=Kc​(T2​)exp[RΔHRx∘​​(T2​1​−T1​)]
  6. Equilibrium conversions [express conc. w.r.t. X and use Kc​=[reactants][products]​]. (sketches: endothermic — Xeq​ rising and XEB​ falling, crossing at Te​; exothermic — Xeq​ falling and XEB​ rising, crossing at Te​.)
    • Te​ → adiabatic eq. temp.; Xe​ → adiabatic eq. conversion (max. conversion one can achieve for a given entering temperature T0​ & feed composition).
    • X∝ flow rate (X=f(Kc​), Kc​=f(ΔH∘,T)). So Xe​ can only be affected by changing T (which can be done by adding inerts) or by reactor staging (adding interstage cooling or heating).
  7. Heat load: heat-exchange duty to cool the reacting mixture from T0​ to T: Q˙​=FA0​cp​(T0​−T).
  8. Eq. and reaction rate always go opposite: higher feed T will have a higher reaction rate (r∝k; k=f(T)). However, XEB​=α(T−T0​) and the intersection of Xeq​ & XEB​ will be lower, giving lower Xe​.
    • For a PFR & PBR, the Xe​ and XEB​ change along the reactor as the temp. in the reactor also changes.
    • Although it may seem that a lower T will have higher Xe​, the actual X of the reactor might even be 0 as the rate is very slow and the reactants fail to react for a given length/catalyst weight of reactor.
    • (sketch: X vs. T — the falling Xeq​ curve and parallel XEB​ lines shifting right as the feed T is increased.)

Chapter 12 [non-isothermal reactors]

For PFR: ΔQ˙​=UΔA(Ta​−T). The differential energy balance, with the product rule giving Hi​dVdFi​​ (from the mole balance, dVdFi​​=ri​) +Fi​dVdHi​​ (=cp​dVdT​), and Fi​=FA0​(Θi​+νi​X):

  1. dVdT​=∑Fi​cpi​​rA​ΔHRx​​Qg​​−Ua(T−Ta​)​Qr​​​ — exothermic: Qg​>0; endothermic: Qg​<0
  2. dVdT​=FA0​(∑Θi​cpi​​+Δcp​X)rA​ΔHRx​−Ua(T−Ta​)​ (as f(X))
  3. For PBR: dWdT​=∑Fi​cpi​​rA′​ΔHRx​−ρb​Ua(T−Ta​)​​; W=ρB​⋅V, ρB​ = density of catalyst

Page 16 — “Gaurav the legend: CBE 142”

  • Michaelis–Menten (all cases) → know how to derive it!
  • Energy balance: ∂t∂E​=Q˙​+W˙s​−FA0​∑Θi​c~pi​​(T−T0​)−FA0​XA​[ΔHrxn∘​+Δc^p​(T−Tr​)]​ (Δc^p​ = molar; c~p​=T2​−T1​1​∫T1​T2​​cp​(T)dT ↳ in our class is the same as cpi​​)
  • ΔHrxn∘​=ΔHrxn​, ΔHrxn​≫Δc~p​(T−Tr​) ∴ adiabatic: XA​=ΔHrxn​∑Θi​c~pi​​(T−T0​)​; T≈T0​+(∑Θi​cpi​​−ΔHrxn​​)XA​

Transcriber’s note: the adiabatic XA​ should carry −ΔHrxn​ in the denominator, as in the T expression beside it.

Wall-cooled CSTR: 0=UA(Ta​−T)−XA​FA0​ΔHrxn​−FA0​∑Θi​cpi​​(T−T0​) ∴

XA​=ΔHrxn​(FA0​UA​+cˉp0​​)(T∗−T)​​;cp0​​=cˉp​=∑Θi​cpi​​;T∗=1+κT0​+κTa​​;κ=cˉp​FA0​UA​

(ΔHrxn​=ΔHrxn∘​ as Δc~p​→0.) If κ = 0, UA=0 ∴ adiabatic.

(sketch: XAMB​ vs. T — the S-shaped G(T) from the MB and energy-balance lines from (T0​,Ta​) for κ = 0, large κ and κ = ∞, for exo and endo.) All the κ move towards κ = ∞ (for both endo & exothermic). Endo cannot have multiple S.S.

★ PFR: q−FA0​dVdT​(cˉp0​​+Δc~p​XA​)−FA0​dVdXA​​(ΔHrxn∘​+Δc^p​(T−Tr​))=0; q=UaV​(Ta​−T)=U(D4​)(Ta​−T).

Page 19 — energy balance on exchangers; CSTR

  1. Energy balance on exchangers (c = coolant): co-current dVdTa​​=m˙c​cpc​​Ua(T−Ta​)​; counter-current dVdTa​​=m˙c​cpc​​Ua(Ta​−T)​. This is information on how Ta​ is changing with the length of the reactor (Ta​ is assumed to be no longer constant).

  2. For a CSTR (W by stirrer is neglected; we assume that there is no accumulation of energy in the heat exchanger):

X=[−ΔHRx∘​(TR​)]FA0​UA​(T−Ta​)+∑Θi​cpi​​(T−T0​)​;T=Tc​+cp0​​(1+κ)(−ΔHRx∘​)X​;κ=(FA0​cp0​​)UA​;Tc​=1+κκTa​+T0​​;cp0​​=∑Θi​cpi​​;V=−rA​(X,T)FA0​X​

where Ta​ → coolant temp. (inlet T = outlet T); TR​ → reference T; T0​ → feed inlet temp.

@ steady state, no accumulation and EB = MB. A CSTR is defined by (X,T,V). (sketch: X vs. T — the S-shaped XMB​ and the straight XEB​.)

XMB​=1+τkτk​,k=f(T);XEB​=−[ΔHRx∘​(TR​)+Δcp​(T−TR​)]∑Θi​cpi​​(T−Ti0​)​(adiabatic)

Pages 21–22 — stoichiometry

For a given reaction aA+bB→cC+dD we can construct a stoich. table (having initial moles, change in moles after reaction & remaining no. of moles). If A is the limiting reagent, then NC​=NC0​+ac​(NA0​⋅X) (X = conversion).

δ=(ad​+ac​−ab​−1)=moles of A reactedchange in the total no. of moles​∴NT​=NT0​+δ(NA0​X)

To get conc. (if V=V0​): CC​=VNC​​=VNC0​+(c/a)NA0​X​=V0​NA0​(NC0​/NA0​+(c/a)X)​; Θ=NA0​NC0​​:

CC​=CA0​(ΘC​+ac​X)​→therefore for a constant-volume reactor we can express concentration as a function of conversion⇒−rA​=f(XA​)

ΘC​=1 (reaction is equimolar); ΘC​=ab​ (stoichiometric); Θi​=NA0​Ni0​​=CA0​Ci0​​=yA0​yi0​​​.

Don’t forget to choose the limiting reagent as the basis for calculation (A).

From the stoich. table (just the stoich. balance, which gives moles of species), we get the total no. of moles as FT​=FT0​+FA0​δX; ÷FT0​ ⇒ FT0​FT​​=1+FT0​FA0​​δX=1+εyA0​δ​​X; ε=yA0​δ​ — ε=total moles fedΔ total moles for complete conversion​.

Flow systems are very similar to batch systems.

  • Varying V and v0​. The same stoich. tables work! (Only have to take care when considering concentration as a f(XA​).) ↳ Most gas-phase reactions (j = species; T = total):
CT​=ZRTP​(CT0​=Z0​RT0​P0​​)∴v0​v​=(FT0​/CT0​)(FT​/CT​)​;v0​v​=FT0​FT​​(T0​T​)(PP0​​)​ Cj​=vFj​​=vFT​​=CT0​(v0​FT0​​)​​(FT​FA​​)(P0​P​)(TT0​​);Cj​=(CT0​)(FT​Fj​​)(P0​P​)(TT0​​)​⇒Cj​=CT0​yj​pTT0​​

As defined earlier, FT0​FT​​=(1+εX) & Fj​=FA0​(Θj​+νj​X) ← general eq. from the stoich. table.

Page 23 — things to know

Damköhler number: a dimensionless number that can give a quick estimate of the degree of conversion that can be achieved in a CSTR.

Da=FA0​−rA0​V​=entering flow rate of Arate of reaction at entrance​="convection rate of A""reaction rate of A"​
  • First order (irreversible reaction): Da1​=FA0​−rA0​V​=v0​CA0​k1​CA0​V​=τk1​
  • 2nd order: Da=FA0​−rA0​V​=v0​CA0​k2​CA02​V​=τk2​CA0​
  • For irreversible reactions: Da<0.1⇒X<0.1; Da>10⇒X>0.9

CSTR in series: In − out + generation = accumulation: FA0​−FA​+rA​V=0 ⇒ rA​V=FA0​−FA0​(1−X); rA​V=FA0​X (rA​=−kCA​). Conversion: FA​=FA0​(1−X); CA​=CA0​(1−X).

V=rA​FA0​X​(÷v0​):τ=rA​CA0​X​=(1−X)rA​CA0​X​⇒τ=k(1−X)X​​;τk=(1−X)X​;X=1+τkτk​​

Now, CA​=CA0​(1−1+τkτk​).
